title: Streaming backpressure interop regression — hosted API (P0)
content:
Summary:

On 2027-06-09 at ~09:23 UTC we observed a P0 degradation affecting streaming responses from the hosted API. Symptoms were high tail latency for streaming sessions (>1000ms per chunk), occasional 5xx errors returned mid-stream, and a large number of client-initiated reconnects. The incident lasted until ~12:05 UTC when a configuration rollback and targeted throttling eliminated the failure mode. Estimated customer impact: increased error rate for streaming clients (peak 8% 5xx on streaming endpoints), slow delivery of tokens causing UX degradation for interactive apps.

High-level impact:
- Time window: 2027-06-09 09:23 UTC -> 12:05 UTC
- Affected surface: Hosted API streaming endpoints (chat and streaming generate)
- Error spike: streaming 5xx rate peaked at 8% (baseline ~0.1%)
- Latency: p99 per-chunk delivery rose from ~120ms -> ~1100ms
- Outbound reconnects: +62% relative to baseline

Immediate detection and response:
- 09:24 UTC: automated alert for streaming p99 token latency triggered (SRE oncall: Diego).
- 09:28 UTC: paging routed to streaming and edge teams. Initial triage focused on autoscaler behavior and kernel queue depth.
- 09:42 UTC: correlation found between elevated client-side buffering events and a recent rollout (canary) that changed stream chunk size negotiation and keepalive handling.
- 10:05 UTC: we rolled back the canary to previous streaming negotiation defaults for the region experiencing highest error rate (eu-west-1). Error rate decreased but latency remained elevated.
- 10:35 UTC: applied temporary throttling (connection admission control) at the edge for long-lived connections from the problematic canary cohort; p95/p99 latencies began to trend down.
- 11:12 UTC: identified a mismatch in backpressure semantics between client SDK v2.3.1 and server-side streaming change in runtime v1.14. The server assumed the client would signal readiness after each N-byte chunk; some clients were using a coalescing buffer and sending readiness less frequently. This caused server-side batching and KV cache contention, leading to head-of-line blocking and occasional connection tear-downs (5xx) when kernel timeouts were hit.
- 11:40 UTC: permanent rollback of the negotiation change across all canaries was initiated; 12:05 UTC: key metrics returned to near-baseline. Incident declared mitigated at 12:10 UTC.

Root cause hypothesis (summary):
- Primary cause: regression in streaming negotiation logic delivered in a canary that changed the expected client backpressure cadence (server began to batch larger chunks and relied on per-chunk readiness signals).
- Secondary factors: server batching interacting badly with KV cache eviction under high concurrency; small VM/network jitter pushed some in-flight timers past our internal kernel timeouts which surfaced as 5xx. Edge admission controls were insufficient to prevent concentrated load from the canary cohort.

Detailed analysis:
- Negotiation diff: the canary introduced a new header/handshake flag (X-Stream-Flow: aggressive) enabling larger chunk sizes and delayed readiness ACK semantics. This was intended to improve throughput but assumed client SDKs had a readiness coalescing path.
- Client interop: ~18% of streaming sessions in the affected region used older SDKs (v2.3.1 and earlier) or custom clients that do not implement the readiness ACK behavior. Those clients therefore did not interoperate with the new semantics, resulting in the server accumulating requests in its batching pipeline.
- KV cache pressure: increased batching length caused per-request KV cache entries to be held longer, which, under peak concurrency, triggered eviction cascades and lock contention. When the runtime tried to recover, some request handlers hit a kernel-level timeout (observed in logs as rpc.ErrDeadlineExceeded) and returned 5xx to clients.
- Observability gaps: our canary rollout telemetry captured success/failure rates but did not correlate per-session SDK-version signals with the handshake flag. That correlation would have allowed faster root cause identification.

Why the rollback and throttle helped:
- Rolling back removed the server-side assumption that clients would provide delayed readiness semantics, returning the flow-control path to a per-chunk readiness model. This reduced batching length and KV cache hold times.
- Admission control prevented the worst cohort of long-lived connections from monopolizing executor capacity while we stabilized the runtime.

Immediate mitigations completed during response:
- Rollback of handshake flag across canaries in the affected region (10:05 UTC -> 11:40 UTC ongoing).
- Edge admission control: temporary limit on long-lived streaming sessions per node for the canary cohort (10:35 UTC).
- Hotline to top downstream SDK maintainers to publish compatibility guidance and patch (11:50 UTC).

Longer-term remediation and action items (owners & due dates):
- SRE: Add per-session SDK-version and handshake-flag correlation to streaming rollout dashboards (owner: Diego Chen) — due 2027-06-25.
- Serving runtime: revert the aggressive batching optimization and harden KV cache hold-time limits with time-based eviction backstops (owner: Lucas Grant) — due 2027-07-02.
- SDK team: publish patch to SDKs to implement explicit readiness ACK semantics and backpressure testing harness (owner: Priya Nair) — due 2027-06-18.
- Rollout process: require compatibility test matrix tying handshake flags to top N SDK versions before canary rollouts (owner: Platform Engineering) — due 2027-06-30.
- Monitoring: create an alert for sudden divergence between stream chunk size distribution and per-chunk readiness frequency (owner: Observability team / Maya Patel) — due 2027-06-20.
- Incident review: schedule cross-team retro with Sampled customers to review UX impact and communication (owner: Customer Success) — due 2027-06-16.

Runbook draft additions (oncall playbook snippets):
- Detection:
  - If streaming p99 chunk latency > 500ms AND streaming 5xx rate > 1% for >5min, trigger streaming severity page.
  - Pull per-session headers: X-Client-SDK-Version, X-Stream-Flow, and stream-chunk-size histogram.
- Immediate steps:
  1) Identify recent rollouts (git_rev, canary cohort) and roll back handshake flags if present.
  2) Enable edge connection admission control for suspect cohort (limit long-lived sessions to N per node).
  3) If rollback not possible quickly, scale dedicated streaming executors and increase KV cache size temporarily to reduce eviction pressure.
- If 5xx originates from rpc.ErrDeadlineExceeded in runtime logs, bail out to rollback and throttle; escalate to runtime owners.

Observability & dashboards to add:
- Session-level scatter: chunk-size vs readiness-frequency annotated by SDK-version.
- KV cache hold-time histogram by executor and region.
- Per-canary cohort streaming error budget burn rate.

Communication notes (customer & internal):
- Customer-facing: Customer Success sent a brief status update at 12:30 UTC summarizing impact and confirming mitigation; follow-up with a detailed post-incident customer note once remediation milestones are completed.
- Internal: Slack incident channel #inc-1723 remained active; consolidate learnings and place final incident summary in Confluence linked above.

Lessons learned (short):
- Protocol-level changes that alter backpressure semantics require explicit, automated compatibility checks with historical client versions before canary rollout.
- Batching improvements can create downstream resource retention effects (cache hold time) that are not visible until under contended load; add synthetic tests that exercise high-concurrency streaming with mixed client versions.
- Edge admission controls and graceful degradation knobs (e.g., per-node long-lived connection caps) are valuable safety valves and should be on-by-default in canary regions.

Appendix: logs & traces to consult during follow-up:
- Runtime traces: trace IDs sampled between 2027-06-09T09:20:00Z and 2027-06-09T12:10:00Z with rpc.ErrDeadlineExceeded annotations.
- Edge logs: connection handshake histories showing X-Stream-Flow header values.
- Canary rollout manifest: serving-runtime:v1.14-canary-15 — compare handshake flag diff against v1.14-stable.

Status of action items (at last_modified):
- Rollback completed: yes.
- Temporary admission control: yes (removed after stability confirmed).
- Observability tasks: in progress.
